newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Tired Mir crew told to rest after blunder.
newsitem.headline: Tired Mir crew told to rest after blunder.

text.p: The crew of the troubled Mir space station have been told to rest so as to recover strength and concentration they badly need to repair damage caused by their own blunders.
Early on Thursday, just three weeks after the worst accident in Mir's 11 years in space, a cosmonaut mistakenly unplugged a vital computer cable and plunged the craft into darkness.

The error forced the three-man Russian-U.S. crew, whose commander developed a heart problem this week, to flee to their Soyuz escape capsule to communicate with Earth. They had to use flashlights to get around the darkened station.
Light, heating and life-support systems were shut down in the main station but, thanks to the escape capsule, they were in no immediate danger.

"We are not planning to return the crew, we are planning to continue the flight," mission director Vladimir Solovyov told reporters after a tense day at Mission Control outside Moscow. "The crew are now being sent to sleep, they are tired."
"This was purely human error," he said, adding angrily: "This is a kindergarten!".

Solovyov said Mir's orientation towards the sun would be restored on Friday morning and the gyrodines system that keeps the station in the best position to accumulate solar energy would be back in operation on Saturday.
Earth and the Russian-U.S. crew restored a computer link on Thursday allowing experts to analyse data and help the cosmonauts repair the craft.

The crew have canned oxygen that will last for just five days, while the temperature and humidity will remain bearable for two or three days without power. This sets a clear time limit on re-starting Mir's life-support machines, including the oxygen generators.
The gyrodines system was also lost on June 25, when a cargo craft slammed into Mir during a manual docking, piercing the Spektr module and depriving Mir of up to half of its energy.

Without the gyroscopes, the crew had to fire rocket engines on the Soyuz craft -- thereby running down the fuel they have to spare to get home if things go wrong. But a spokesman said escape capsule was burning little fuel and had plenty left.
Solovyov said Mir commander Vasily Tsibliyev, 43, who is on a course of medication after developing an irregular heartbeat probably caused by stress, needed no less than 10-12 hours of rest.
"He remains commander despite mistakes," Solovyov said of Tsibliyev, declining to say who had made the error.

But Solovyov said the latest crisis probably meant that repair work in the Spektr module to reconnect cables to three solar batteries, cut off during the June collision, would have to be put off once more. He said the date for the work would be decided later.
The sortie to the Spektr had already been put off after Tsibliyev's illness.
NASA physicist Michael Foale, 40, is now due to step in to a spacesuit to help engineer Alexander Lazutkin, 39. NASA cleared Foale to train for the risky operation.

But officials have said the job may now be left for a Russian-French crew due to arrive on Mir on August 7. If the present crew abandoned ship, Mir would die as its systems cannot operate without human hands on the controls.
The series of mishaps has raised questions over whether Mir should be ditched before a new international space station is launched next year.
Russian officials, whose agency depends on the foreign cash Mir brings in to keep much of the post-Soviet space industry aloft, insist they do not want to abandon the station.
